entities.label: Spacewar!
entities.blurb: The MIT PDP-1 dueling-rockets demo that proved computers could host shared playful worlds.

entities.label: Colossal Cave Adventure
entities.blurb: Will Crowther's mapped Kentucky cave in text, the root of every explorable virtual place.

entities.label: Maze War
entities.blurb: NASA Ames students wired Imlac terminals into the first first-person multiplayer shooter.

entities.label: MUD1

milestones.what: licensed to CompuServe as British Legends

entities.blurb: Essex University's Multi-User Dungeon, the shared text world that named an entire genre.

entities.label: Roy Trubshaw
entities.blurb: Essex student who wrote the original MUD in 1978 and handed the world to Richard Bartle.

entities.label: Richard Bartle
entities.blurb: MUD1 co-creator whose player-type taxonomy still frames virtual-world design debates.

entities.label: AberMUD
entities.blurb: Alan Cox's Aberystwyth MUD whose spreading source code seeded the great MUD family trees.

entities.label: TinyMUD
entities.blurb: Jim Aspnes stripped out combat and let players build rooms, tilting MUDs toward social worlds.

entities.label: LambdaMOO
entities.blurb: The programmable text mansion at Xerox PARC where online community governance was invented the hard way.

entities.label: Pavel Curtis
entities.blurb: Xerox PARC researcher who founded and ran LambdaMOO as a living laboratory of online society.

entities.label: DikuMUD

milestones.what: source released from the University of Copenhagen

entities.blurb: Copenhagen's class-and-level combat MUD codebase whose DNA runs straight into EverQuest.

entities.label: Island of Kesmai
entities.blurb: CompuServe's $6-an-hour roguelike island, one of the first commercial multiplayer online RPGs.

entities.label: Neverwinter Nights (AOL)
entities.blurb: Stormfront's AOL D&D world, widely credited as the first graphical MMORPG on a major service.

entities.label: Meridian 59
entities.blurb: The 3DO-published pioneer usually credited as the first 3D MMORPG, a year ahead of Ultima Online.

entities.label: Ultima Online
entities.blurb: Origin's shard-based fantasy world that put 'massively multiplayer' into the industry's vocabulary.

entities.label: Richard Garriott
entities.blurb: Lord British of the Ultima series, who produced Ultima Online and later flew to the ISS.

entities.label: Raph Koster
entities.blurb: MUD-bred lead designer of Ultima Online and virtual-world theorist behind A Theory of Fun.

entities.label: EverQuest
entities.blurb: The DikuMUD-descended 3D world that made subscription MMORPGs a mass business before WoW.

entities.label: Asheron's Call
entities.blurb: Turbine's seamless-world MMO, the third of the big three late-90s MMORPGs, published by Microsoft.

entities.label: RuneScape
entities.blurb: The Gower brothers' browser MMO that quietly amassed hundreds of millions of accounts.

entities.label: Lineage
entities.blurb: NCSoft's castle-siege MMO that built Korea's PC-bang economy and its MMO industry.

entities.label: Ragnarok Online
entities.blurb: Gravity's manhwa-styled MMO that carried Korean online worlds across Asia.

entities.label: EVE Online
entities.blurb: CCP's single-shard spacefaring sandbox where player politics and economics are the content.

entities.label: World of Warcraft
entities.blurb: Blizzard's polished Azeroth turned the MMORPG from hobbyist niche into global mass culture.

entities.label: Blizzard Entertainment
entities.blurb: The Irvine studio whose World of Warcraft defined the mass-market persistent world.

entities.label: Final Fantasy XI
entities.blurb: Square's cross-platform MMO that put console players and PC players in one world in 2002.

entities.label: Final Fantasy XIV

milestones.what: relaunched as A Realm Reborn after the failed 1.0

entities.blurb: The MMO that died at launch, was rebuilt in public, and returned as one of the genre's biggest worlds.

entities.label: Guild Wars
entities.blurb: ArenaNet's instanced, subscription-free challenger launched into the teeth of the WoW era.

entities.label: NCSoft
entities.blurb: The Seoul publisher behind Lineage and Guild Wars that industrialized the Korean MMO.

entities.label: Wolfenstein 3D
entities.blurb: Id's shareware castle run that established the template Doom would detonate a year later.

entities.label: Doom

milestones.what: deathmatch and DWANGO dial-up play spread multiplayer culture
source code released, seeding decades of mods and ports

entities.blurb: The shareware inferno that spawned deathmatch, mod culture, and a decade of 'Doom clones'.

entities.label: Quake

milestones.what: Quake III engine (id Tech 3) licensed for Call of Duty and Medal of Honor

entities.blurb: True-3D internet deathmatch whose engine, licensed far and wide, became the trunk of the id Tech tree.

entities.label: id Software
entities.blurb: The Texas garage band of programmers that invented the modern FPS and licensed its engines to the world.

entities.label: John Carmack
entities.blurb: Engine savant whose Wolfenstein, Doom, and Quake renderers repeatedly redefined real-time 3D.

entities.label: John Romero
entities.blurb: Id co-founder and Doom designer who evangelized deathmatch and player-made levels.

entities.label: GoldSrc
entities.blurb: Valve's heavily rebuilt Quake engine, the substrate of Half-Life and the Counter-Strike mod boom.

entities.label: Half-Life
entities.blurb: Valve's scripted-story shooter whose open mod tools made it a platform as much as a game.

entities.label: Counter-Strike
entities.blurb: The Half-Life mod by two amateurs that became the definitive proof of mod culture's power.

entities.label: Valve
entities.blurb: The Half-Life studio that became PC gaming's landlord through Steam.

entities.label: Steam

milestones.what: Half-Life 2 made Steam mandatory, forcing adoption

entities.blurb: Valve's update pipe turned storefront that became the default distribution layer for PC worlds.

entities.label: Unreal Engine

milestones.what: UE4 made free with royalties, exploding adoption

entities.blurb: Epic's licensed engine dynasty, from the 1998 shooter Unreal to the substrate of Fortnite and film sets.

entities.label: Epic Games
entities.blurb: Tim Sweeney's shareware outfit that grew into the Unreal Engine and Fortnite juggernaut.

entities.label: Tim Sweeney
entities.blurb: From ZZT in his parents' Maryland house to Unreal Engine and an open-metaverse crusade.

entities.label: ZZT
entities.blurb: Sweeney's ANSI-art game that shipped with its own world editor, breeding a user-creation community.

entities.label: Unreal Tournament
entities.blurb: Epic's arena shooter that met Quake III head-on in the winter of 1999's great FPS duel.

entities.label: Source Engine
entities.blurb: Valve's Half-Life 2 engine whose SDK powered a generation of mods, from Garry's Mod outward.

entities.label: Super Mario 64
entities.blurb: The analog-stick playground that taught the whole industry how to move a camera through 3D space.

entities.label: Nintendo
entities.blurb: The Kyoto card company turned console titan whose Mario 64 defined navigable 3D worlds.

entities.label: Garry's Mod
entities.blurb: A physics sandbox with no goal that became a factory for player-invented game modes.

entities.label: Roblox
entities.blurb: A physics-toy descendant that became the largest user-generated game universe on Earth.

entities.label: David Baszucki
entities.blurb: Physics-simulation entrepreneur who watched students play with Interactive Physics and built Roblox.

entities.label: Knowledge Revolution
entities.blurb: Baszucki's educational software firm whose Interactive Physics sim was Roblox's conceptual ancestor.

entities.label: Minecraft
entities.blurb: Notch's block world, inspired by Infiniminer, that became the best-selling game ever made.

entities.label: Markus "Notch" Persson
entities.blurb: The indie programmer whose weekend block game outsold everything in gaming history.

entities.label: Mojang
entities.blurb: The Stockholm studio built around Minecraft and sold to Microsoft for $2.5 billion.

entities.label: Microsoft
entities.blurb: The platform giant that published Asheron's Call, bought Mojang, and swallowed ZeniMax and id.

entities.label: Dreams
entities.blurb: Media Molecule's console creation suite where players sculpted whole games inside a game.

entities.label: Fortnite

milestones.what: pivoted from co-op survival to Battle Royale
Travis Scott concert drew over 12M concurrent players

entities.blurb: The survival game that pivoted to battle royale, then pivoted again into a concert hall and creator platform.

entities.label: Unreal Editor for Fortnite
entities.blurb: Epic put Unreal Engine tooling inside Fortnite and started paying creators from the ecosystem's revenue.

entities.label: Core
entities.blurb: Manticore's bid to give Roblox-style creators the fidelity of Unreal Engine.

entities.label: Unity

milestones.what: iPhone support sparked the mobile indie wave
runtime-fee pricing revolt and CEO exit

entities.blurb: The Mac-born engine that democratized game development and quietly powers much of the social-VR metaverse.

entities.label: David Helgason
entities.blurb: Unity co-founder and CEO through 2014 who preached the democratization of game development.

entities.label: Godot

milestones.what: adoption surge amid Unity's pricing backlash

entities.blurb: The MIT-licensed community engine that became the open-source refuge of the engine wars.

entities.label: RenderWare
entities.blurb: Criterion's middleware workhorse of the PS2 era, effectively retired from the market after EA bought it.

entities.label: CryEngine
entities.blurb: Crytek's benchmark-setting engine, licensed outward to worlds as unlikely as Blue Mars.

entities.label: Sony
entities.blurb: The PlayStation giant whose online arm ran EverQuest and whose Media Molecule built Dreams.
